newsitem.title: GERMANY: Opinion-formers reassure Germans on euro currency.
newsitem.headline: Opinion-formers reassure Germans on euro currency.

text.p: German opinion-formers on Saturday lauded the "stability pact" for Europe's planned single currency, giving Chancellor Helmut Kohl a boost in his fight to reassure citizens worried about giving up the mark.

Correspondents and commentators from newspapers and television rallied behind the agreement struck in Dublin, which lays down sanctions and fines for countries which take part in monetary union but then fail to meet annual budget targets.
"The chances that the single currency will be as hard as the mark have risen because of the stability pact," the liberal Frankfurter Rundschau newspaper said in an editorial.
"In a fight which was practically one side against everyone else, Bonn has done more than just save face."

The praise could scarcely have come at a better time for Kohl, the driving force behind European integration, who has found his compatriots increasingly anxious about giving up their beloved rock-hard national currency.
Just a few days ago, a survey found 61 percent of Germans looked forward with fear to economic and monetary union (EMU) while only 16 percent were hopeful about the euro currency.

But Saturday's papers, while expressing a few reservations, gave a broad welcome to Friday's agreement, with both the Frankfurter Allgeimeine Zeitung and Die Welt saying agreement had been reached on "the stability pact demanded by Germany".

The future euro-bills, also unveiled in Dublin, were featured on the front page of almost all Saturday's newspapers. Bild, Germany's biggest-selling daily, said the designs had made the currency "beautiful, really European".
Friday evening television programmes had already set the tone for Saturday's positive coverage.

Germany's most-watched evening news programme, ARD television's Tagesschau, broke with its long-established staid format by beginning with pictures of how the new currency will look even before the presenter had welcomed viewers.
The public broadcaster's weekly political magazine programme, Bericht aus Bonn, also gave the pact major coverage.

"The stability pact has been agreed. Admittedly, it doesn't look quite like (Finance Minister) Theo Waigel wanted but it's here and that means an important hurdle on the road to monetary union has been overcome," anchorman Rolf-Dieter Krause said.

The programme's correspondent in Dublin, Dierk Schaaf, said the compromise pact was none the worse for taking on board the views of other countries and not imposing all the automatic sanctions which Bonn would have liked.
"I think the compromise is at least no worse than what Waigel wanted," he said. "It's a bit different from what Waigel was looking for but that doesn't mean it's any less good."
